concepts.description_formal: For a rate function f on [a,b], the signed area between the graph of f and the x axis over [a,b] equals the accumulated change in the antiderivative quantity over [a,b].
concepts.description_plain: The area between a rate of change graph and the horizontal axis measures how much the quantity changed.
concepts.name: Accumulation of change as area under a rate graph
concepts.notation: signed area; accumulated change

concepts.description_formal: If f is positive (negative) on an interval the accumulated change is positive (negative); the unit of the accumulation is the unit of f multiplied by the unit of the independent variable.
concepts.description_plain: The sign of the rate fixes the sign of the accumulated change, and the units multiply.
concepts.name: Sign and units of accumulated change
concepts.notation: units of f times units of t

concepts.description_formal: For a partition of [a,b] into subintervals of widths delta x sub i, a Riemann sum is the sum of f(x sub i star) times delta x sub i, where x sub i star is chosen as a left endpoint, right endpoint, or midpoint; a trapezoidal sum averages the two endpoint values on each subinterval.
concepts.description_plain: A definite integral can be estimated by adding function value times subinterval width over a partition.
concepts.name: Riemann sum approximation of a definite integral
concepts.notation: L sub n, R sub n, M sub n, T sub n

concepts.description_formal: For a monotone integrand, a left Riemann sum underestimates when f is increasing and overestimates when f is decreasing, with the reverse for a right sum; for a concave up integrand a trapezoidal sum overestimates and a midpoint sum underestimates.
concepts.description_plain: Whether an approximation is too big or too small follows from how the function rises, falls, or bends.
concepts.name: Over and under estimate reasoning for approximations
concepts.notation: underestimate, overestimate

concepts.description_formal: A Riemann sum over a partition of an interval I is the sum from i = 1 to n of f(x sub i star) times delta x sub i, where each term is a function value at a point of a subinterval multiplied by the length of that subinterval.
concepts.description_plain: Sigma notation writes a Riemann sum compactly as a sum of products.
concepts.name: Summation notation and the Riemann sum as a sum of products
concepts.notation: sigma from i = 1 to n

concepts.description_formal: The definite integral of a continuous f over [a,b] is the limit of Riemann sums as the maximum subinterval width approaches 0, written as the integral from a to b of f(x) dx.
concepts.description_plain: Letting every subinterval width go to zero turns the Riemann sum into the definite integral.
concepts.name: Definite integral as the limit of Riemann sums
concepts.notation: integral from a to b of f(x) dx

concepts.description_formal: For f continuous on an interval containing a, g(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt defines a function g on that interval; t is a bound variable and x is the independent variable.
concepts.description_plain: A definite integral with a variable upper limit defines a new function of that limit.
concepts.name: Accumulation function defined by a definite integral
concepts.notation: g(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt

concepts.description_formal: If f is continuous on an interval containing a, then the derivative with respect to x of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt equals f(x) for x in that interval; when the upper limit is u(x) the chain rule gives f(u(x)) times u'(x).
concepts.description_plain: Differentiating an accumulation function returns the integrand evaluated at the upper limit.
concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part one
concepts.notation: d/dx of integral from a to x of f(t) dt = f(x)

concepts.description_formal: For g(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt, the sign of f gives the monotonicity of g, sign changes of f give relative extrema of g, and the monotonicity of f gives the concavity and points of inflection of g.
concepts.description_plain: The graph of the integrand controls where the accumulation function rises, falls, and bends.
concepts.name: Behaviour of an accumulation function read from the integrand
concepts.notation: g', g'' in terms of f, f'

concepts.description_formal: If the graph of f over [a,b] consists of segments and circular arcs, the integral from a to b of f(x) dx is the sum of the areas of the regions above the axis minus the areas of the regions below the axis.
concepts.description_plain: When the graph is made of lines and circular arcs the integral is a sum of signed areas.
concepts.name: Definite integral evaluated by geometry
concepts.notation: signed area

concepts.description_formal: Properties of definite integrals include the integral of a constant times a function, the integral of a sum, reversal of the limits of integration, the integral over adjacent intervals, and the vanishing integral over a degenerate interval; the definition extends to integrands with removable or jump discontinuities.
concepts.description_plain: Constants factor out, sums split, reversing the limits flips the sign, and adjacent intervals add.
concepts.name: Algebraic properties of the definite integral
concepts.notation: integral from a to b = minus integral from b to a

concepts.description_formal: If f is continuous on [a,b] and F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals F(b) minus F(a); equivalently the net change in F over [a,b] is the integral of its rate.
concepts.description_plain: An antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints gives the exact integral and the net change.
concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part two and net change
concepts.notation: F(b) - F(a)

concepts.description_formal: The average value of f over [a,b] is one over (b minus a) times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx.
concepts.description_plain: The average value divides the accumulated amount by the length of the interval.
concepts.name: Average value of a function
concepts.notation: 1/(b-a) times integral from a to b

concepts.description_formal: The integral of f(x) dx equals F(x) plus C where F'(x) = f(x) and C is any constant; differentiation rules read backwards give the basic antiderivative forms, and many functions have no closed-form antiderivative.
concepts.description_plain: An indefinite integral names the whole family of functions whose derivative is the integrand.
concepts.name: Antiderivative and indefinite integral
concepts.notation: integral of f(x) dx = F(x) + C

concepts.description_formal: If u = g(x) and du = g'(x) dx, then the integral of f(g(x)) g'(x) dx equals the integral of f(u) du; for a definite integral the limits of integration must be converted to u values or the antiderivative back-substituted before evaluation.
concepts.description_plain: Naming an inner expression u converts a composite integrand into a basic form.
concepts.name: Substitution of variables
concepts.notation: u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx

concepts.description_formal: Techniques for finding antiderivatives include rearrangements into equivalent forms, such as long division of an improper rational function and completing the square in a quadratic denominator to reach a logarithmic or inverse trigonometric form.
concepts.description_plain: Long division and completing the square turn an unworkable integrand into a standard one.
concepts.name: Rearrangement into an equivalent integrable form
concepts.notation: quotient plus remainder over divisor

concepts.description_formal: Integration by parts states that the integral of u dv equals u v minus the integral of v du, and is the product rule for derivatives read as an antidifferentiation technique.
concepts.description_plain: Parts trades one integral for a simpler one using the product rule in reverse.
concepts.name: Integration by parts
concepts.notation: integral u dv = uv - integral v du

concepts.description_formal: Some rational functions can be decomposed into sums of ratios with linear, nonrepeating denominators, each of which antidifferentiates to a constant times a natural logarithm of the linear factor.
concepts.description_plain: A rational function with distinct linear factors splits into simple fractions that integrate to logarithms.
concepts.name: Linear partial fraction decomposition
concepts.notation: A/(x-r) + B/(x-s)

concepts.description_formal: An improper integral has one or both limits infinite or an integrand unbounded on the interval of integration; it is evaluated as a limit of definite integrals, converging when that limit exists and diverging otherwise.
concepts.description_plain: An integral with an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand is defined as a limit of ordinary integrals.
concepts.name: Improper integral and convergence
concepts.notation: limit as b approaches infinity of integral from a to b

concepts.description_formal: Classification of an integrand by its structure, such as a composite with an available inner derivative, a product of unlike factors, an improper rational form, or a factorable linear denominator, determines which antidifferentiation procedure applies.
concepts.description_plain: The structure of the integrand decides which technique applies.
concepts.name: Selecting an antidifferentiation technique
concepts.notation: technique classification

prerequisites.description_plain: Factoring constants out, splitting a fraction into terms, and rewriting a product so that one factor is a constant multiple of the derivative of another expression.
prerequisites.failure_signature: Student cannot see that the integrand is a composite times the derivative of the inner expression and attempts term-by-term antidifferentiation.
prerequisites.name: Rewriting expressions to expose an inner function and its derivative
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Converting radicals and reciprocals to powers, adding exponents on products, and applying the power rule in reverse to any real exponent other than negative one.
prerequisites.failure_signature: Radical or reciprocal integrands are left unrewritten, or the power rule is applied to an exponent of negative one.
prerequisites.name: Exponent rules including negative and fractional exponents
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms, the domain of ln, and the use of absolute value inside the logarithm of a linear expression.
prerequisites.failure_signature: Logarithmic answers are not combined or simplified, or ln of a negative quantity is written without absolute value.
prerequisites.name: Logarithm rules and properties of the natural logarithm
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Pythagorean identities, double angle identities, and the reciprocal and quotient identities used to rewrite an integrand into a form whose antiderivative is a basic trigonometric function.
prerequisites.failure_signature: A squared trigonometric integrand is antidifferentiated as if it were a basic form instead of being rewritten first.
prerequisites.name: Trigonometric identities used in antidifferentiation
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Interpreting f(t), f'(x), f(g(x)), and evaluation at a stated input, and distinguishing a function from its value at a point.
prerequisites.failure_signature: Values are pulled from a table or a graph for the wrong input, or f' and f are interchanged.
prerequisites.name: Reading function notation, composition, and evaluation
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Expanding and writing sigma notation with an index, lower and upper limits, and a general term.
prerequisites.failure_signature: The index is not substituted correctly, or the number of terms is off by one.
prerequisites.name: Summation notation
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Computing the areas of rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, and circular or semicircular regions from lengths read off a figure.
prerequisites.failure_signature: A trapezoidal region is treated as a rectangle, or a semicircular region is given the area of a full circle.
prerequisites.name: Area formulas for rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, circles, and semicircles
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Comparing an approximation with an exact quantity and stating which is larger, given the direction in which a function rises, falls, or bends.
prerequisites.failure_signature: An over or under estimate claim is asserted without reference to monotonicity or concavity.
prerequisites.name: Inequality reasoning about approximations
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Dividing one polynomial by another to write an improper rational expression as a polynomial plus a proper remainder term.
prerequisites.failure_signature: An improper rational integrand is antidifferentiated directly without division.
prerequisites.name: Polynomial long division
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Rewriting a quadratic as a perfect square plus or minus a constant in order to expose a standard form.
prerequisites.failure_signature: A quadratic denominator is left in general form and no standard antiderivative form is recognised.
prerequisites.name: Completing the square
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Clearing denominators and either substituting convenient values or equating coefficients to solve a small linear system for the numerators of a decomposition.
prerequisites.failure_signature: The decomposition constants are guessed or left unsolved.
prerequisites.name: Solving for undetermined coefficients in a rational identity
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Computing each subinterval width as a difference of consecutive partition points rather than assuming a single common width.
prerequisites.failure_signature: One common width is used across subintervals of different lengths.
prerequisites.name: Arithmetic with nonuniform subinterval widths
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.

prerequisites.description_plain: Recognising that the variable of integration is internal to the integral and that only the limits carry the outside variable.
prerequisites.failure_signature: The variable of integration is treated as the independent variable of the accumulation function.
prerequisites.name: Bound variables and the dummy variable convention
prerequisites.notes: Non-calculus prerequisite inferred from the demands of the Unit 6 essential knowledge statements.
